title: Formula 1 looks at 3.0 L V8 turbos and smaller hybrids for 2030
gist: Formula 1's 2026 near-50:50 hybrid rules overreached on battery capability, forcing mid-cycle patches (engine power up, electric down, shorter races in 2027, 60:40 split in 2028), and stakeholders have preliminarily agreed to replace them with 3.0 L turbo V8s and a heavily downsized hybrid (roughly 100 kW electric assist) as early as 2030. The retreat marks a reversal of the electrification optimism that attracted Audi, Cadillac, and Ford, and an early switch would strand current power-unit investments, hitting Cadillac hardest.

insights.claim: Formula 1's 2026 power units use a 4 MJ (1.1 kWh) battery that can sustain full-throttle electric deployment for only about 11-12 seconds, while even the shortest 2026 lap took over 66 seconds, leaving the electric side badly undersized for a full lap.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that current battery energy density cannot support aggressive electrification in weight/size-constrained high-performance vehicles.
insights.quote: the 4 MJ (1.1 kWh) battery can last maybe 11 or 12 seconds at full throttle
insights.locator: But an F1 car is of limited size

insights.claim: Many classic Formula 1 circuits lack enough braking zones for regenerative braking to recover more than a fraction of a lap's energy demand, so cars resort to 'super clipping', diverting up to 250 kW from the V6 to charge the battery at the cost of rear-wheel power.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Energy-recovery limits, not motor power, are the binding constraint in hybrid performance design.
insights.locator: Regenerative braking isn’t the only way

insights.claim: Under the 2026 Formula 1 rules, car output swings between about 750 kW and 400 kW depending on battery state, governed largely by opaque deployment algorithms sensitive to driving style, and unexpected torque spikes have caused multiple crashes this season.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Software-controlled energy deployment has created safety and spectacle problems that pressure the sport to de-emphasize electrification.
insights.quote: More than a few times this season, we’ve seen a driver crash after a sudden torque spike they weren’t expecting.
insights.locator: So sometimes an F1 car will have 1,005 hp

insights.claim: Adding a front electric motor would have improved efficiency and energy recapture in Formula 1's 2026 cars, but incumbent power-unit makers allegedly blocked it out of fear of new entrant Audi's all-wheel-drive hybrid expertise.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Incumbent manufacturers' competitive politics shaped technically suboptimal rules, a pattern relevant to how industry standards get set.

insights.claim: Formula 1's qualifying energy-deployment tweaks, meant to reduce dangerous speed differentials, have slowed cars further in the session where they are supposed to be fully flat-out.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Patches to the hybrid rules carry performance costs, adding pressure for a faster overhaul.

insights.claim: For 2027, Formula 1 is raising V6 output to 420 kW and cutting the electric motor from 350 kW to 300 kW (except in boost mode), and because teams cannot afford bigger fuel tanks under the $215 million cost cap, the F1 Commission approved shortening races from 305 km to 290 km.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: The cost cap constrains redesign so tightly that the sport changed race distance rather than cars, a signal of how binding budget limits are for teams.
insights.locator: Next year, the V6 is being turned up

insights.claim: Formula 1 power units will be rebalanced again in 2028 to a 60:40 combustion-to-electric split, a second step back from the 2026 near-50:50 design.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: The sport is steadily reducing its electric share, which weakens its value as a showcase for automaker EV technology.
insights.locator: In 2028, the power units will be rebalanced

insights.claim: The FIA, FOM, teams, and engine manufacturers have preliminarily agreed, per Autosport, that Formula 1's next power units will be 3.0 L turbocharged V8s with a seriously downsized hybrid system, arriving by 2031 at the latest and possibly 2030.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A top motorsport series is retreating from heavy electrification, reflecting the cooling of automaker EV optimism since the 2026 rules were set.
insights.quote: Instead of 1.6 L V6 turbos, the engines will be 3.0 L V8s, still with turbochargers.

insights.claim: The author expects Formula 1's next-generation cars to have only about 100 kW (134 hp) of electric assist, versus 350 kW in the 2026 rules.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A roughly two-thirds cut in electric power would sharply reduce F1's demand for high-performance battery and motor development.
insights.quote: we might expect just 134 hp (100 kW) of electric assist

insights.claim: Naturally aspirated engines were ruled out for Formula 1's next rules mainly because noise limits at many new street circuits would be exceeded, and keeping a turbo and a hybrid lets the sport claim road relevance.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Street-race venue economics and the need for road relevance to keep automakers involved constrain engine choices.
insights.locator: Despite a desire by some fans

insights.claim: Formula 1's next power units must be at least 50 kg lighter than the current 185 kg minimum, helping reverse a two-decade rise in minimum car weight from 605 kg in 2006 to 800 kg in 2025 (768 kg in 2026).
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Weight reduction is a stated design goal, favoring smaller batteries and lighter hybrid components.
insights.locator: Gratifyingly, the next F1 power units

insights.claim: Formula 1 dropped the electric turbocharger in 2026 on cost and complexity grounds, even though electric turbochargers are now appearing on some road cars, and it is unclear whether the next rules will bring it back.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Electric turbo technology is migrating to road cars regardless of F1's choices, so watch whether the next rules re-adopt it for road relevance.
insights.locator: There’s also no mention of whether

insights.claim: Formula 1 is leaning toward an IndyCar-style driver-controlled 'push to pass' boost for its next rules rather than returning to the drag reduction system it dropped at the start of 2026.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Minor rules detail, but still under discussion and relevant to future racing format and spectacle.

insights.claim: Formula 1's 2026 electrification-heavy rules succeeded in attracting manufacturers: Audi, Cadillac, and Ford signed up, joining Mercedes, Ferrari, and Honda, which recommitted after pulling out in 2021.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Manufacturers joined on an EV-relevance premise, so the shift back to V8s tests whether they stay engaged.

insights.claim: Bringing Formula 1's new V8 rules forward to 2030 would force engine manufacturers to write off current power units early, hitting Cadillac hardest because it only plans to introduce its in-house V6 for the 2029 season.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: An accelerated 2030 switch would leave Cadillac's in-house V6 program with about one season of use, stranding the investment.
insights.quote: This would hit Cadillac hardest, as it’s only planning to introduce its in-house V6 for the start of the 2029 season.
